## Abstract

This study examined the GPS-derived match physical outputs of youth soccer players promoted to compete in a higher age category. A retrospective observational study was conducted using match data collected over three seasons (2022–23 to 2024–25) from an elite youth soccer academy (n = 221). Three questions were examined: (i) whether promoted players differed from their regular teammates when competing in their original age category; (ii) whether they differed from the regular players of the higher age category when competing alongside them; and (iii) whether the same promoted players changed their physical outputs between the two age categories. External load variables included relative total distance, high-speed running, sprint distance, high intensity accelerations and decelerations. In their original age category, promoted players did not consistently differ from their regular teammates, although promoted Under-19 midfielders covered greater high-speed running distance. In the higher age category, promoted players generally showed physical outputs similar to those of the regular players of that category, although promoted Under-19 wingers covered greater sprint distance than regular Under-23 wingers. Within-player comparisons, often based on very few players, revealed position- and category-specific changes, with significant effects for decelerations in Under-16 and Under-19 centre-backs, high-speed running and sprint distance in Under-17 full-backs and strikers, and total distance in Under-19 strikers. These findings suggest that promotion is not associated with a consistent change in match physical outputs, but rather with specific changes according to age category, playing position, and physical variable, supporting individualized approaches to player development.

Skilled youth soccer players who mentally simulate penalty kicks using first-person visual perspectives or kinesthetic sensations score more goals and achieve greater shooting accuracy than when using external spectator viewpoints or standard countdown preparations, according to an experimental investigation conducted at the Elite Center of the French Regions of America. Penalty shoot-outs occur in elimination tournaments when teams fail to break ties after regulation and extra time, placing immense psychological pressure on individual shooters through heightened personal, teammate, coaching, and public expectations. ## Abstract

### Background

Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture is one of the most severe injuries in professional soccer players, often leading to long absences from competition and career-threatening consequences. Understanding how return to play (RTP) outcomes have evolved over time is essential for optimizing recovery and minimizing re-injury risk. Following PRISMA guidelines, MEDLINE (PubMed), Embase (Elsevier), and the Cochrane Library were systematically searched on March 8, 2025, and updated on March 22, 2025. linkup.title: How to Do Citation Searching for a Systematic Review
linkup.snippet:
Citation searching is the set of methods that find studies through citation links instead of keywords. You start from papers already known to be relevant, called seed references, and screen the papers they cite (backward) and the papers that cite them (forward).
The TARCiS statement, published in the BMJ in 2024, set out shared terms for the method. It defines backward citation searching as "retrieving and screening cited references", forward citation searching as "retrieving and screening citing references", and seed references as "relevant articles which are known beforehand and used as a starting point for any citation search" [\[1\]](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2023-078384).
- **Reference list checking:**the traditional form of backward citation searching: reading the reference list of each included study.
| Feature | Backward citation searching | Forward citation searching |
| Direction in time | Older papers, published before the seed | Newer papers, published after the seed |
| Source | The seed study's reference list | A citation index or citation tool |
| Typical tools | The full text, or the cited references in a citation index | Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, or a free tool such as citationchaser |
| What it finds | Foundational trials, earlier reports of the same study, studies described in different words | Recent trials, follow-up reports, studies published after your search date |
| Main limit | Only finds what the authors chose to cite | Coverage differs between indexes, and very recent papers have few citations yet |
Backward citation searching examines the reference list of a seed study, so it finds older work the authors cited. Forward citation searching uses a citation index to find later papers that cite the seed, so it finds newer work, including studies published after your database search. Most guidance treats the two as complementary \[1].

linkup.title: Backward vs. Forward Citation Searching: Key Differences
linkup.snippet:
**Backward citation searching** means examining the works cited by your seed paper. In its simplest form, you open the paper's reference list and inspect potentially relevant references. Citation databases and specialized tools can also retrieve these cited references electronically.  
Suppose a paper was published in 2024 and contains 55 references. Those references form its backward citation links.
**Forward citation searching** reverses the direction. Rather than asking what the seed paper cited, you ask which later publications cited the seed paper.  
You cannot normally determine this from the original paper itself. A paper published in 2018 could not have listed a study published in 2025 among its references. You need a citation index or another service that tracks citations after publication.  
Services such as Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science provide forms of forward citation searching, although their coverage and citation records differ. Other scholarly discovery services and dedicated citation-searching tools may provide similar functionality.  
Forward searching can be particularly valuable when the seed paper is older. It lets you see how later researchers used, extended, replicated, challenged, reviewed, or simply cited that work.

octen.snippet:
The purpose of this study was to identify, synthesize and evaluate interventions used in preventing sport-related concussion (SRC) in adult soccer players. Methods: Five databases (MEDLINE, CINAHL, Embase, SPORTDiscus, PsycINFO) were searched on 6 September 2024 and updated on 17 December 2025 for concussion prevention intervention studies involving adult footballers. Study quality was assessed with the Modified Downs and Black Checklist. A narrative synthesis of all included studies followed Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis (SWiM) guidelines. Results: From 3463 records, five studies met inclusion criteria: three reported rule changes and two reported head-neck training interventions. The low volume of studies discovered were non-randomized and rated fair or poor on quality assessment. Whilst these interventions were grounded in sound and well-reasoned mechanisms to mitigate SRC risks, none reported statistically significant directional effects. This, combined with high heterogeneity, prevented data pooling and no firm conclusions could be drawn about the effectiveness of any intervention. Conclusions: Sparce, preliminary, heterogeneous evidence represents research to reduce SRC in adult soccer players, and this is limited to investigating rule changes and head-neck training and interventions. A larger volume of primary research is needed to determine meaningful practice recommendations of these and other conceivable interventions.

Citation searching for a systematic review finds extra studies by checking the reference lists of your included studies (backward citation searching) and the newer papers that cite them (forward citation searching). It supplements your database searches rather than replacing them, and it catches studies your search terms missed.

Citation searching is the set of methods that find studies through citation links instead of keywords. Citation searching for a systematic review finds extra studies by checking the reference lists of your included studies (backward citation searching) and the newer papers that cite them (forward citation searching). It supplements your database searches rather than replacing them, and it catches studies your search terms missed.

A reader should be able to see how many records your searches produced, what happened to each of them, and why the final set of studies is the final set. | Term | PRISMA 2020 definition (Page et al., 2021) | In practice |
| ---- | --------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| Record | The title or abstract (or both) of a report indexed in a database or website | One row in your exported search results |
